extracted.intended_audience: students and young men aspiring to careers in newspapers / journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and professional standards for preparing for and practicing the newspaper profession: education, literary preparation, subject-matter knowledge, and the duties/qualities required in reporters, editors, and specialist staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-class general education (including Greek and Latin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Give the young man a first-class course of general education; every young man going to be a newspaper man should learn Greek and Latin after the good old fashion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author prefers classical studies as foundational — e.g., familiarity with Sophocles, Tacitus, Horace — arguing that these strengthen command of English and general scholarship; avoid scattering the curriculum and instead pursue rigorous classical studies if possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate accuracy in learning and recitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursue those studies that give accuracy in learning, and that give fidelity and accuracy in recitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education's great end is to be able to tell what you know; avoid the anti-pattern of being able to 'tell a great deal you did not know.' Emphasize precise facts (example: knowing two and one quarter vs two and three eighths).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy in reporting facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Be able to get the thing exactly as it is; state it accurately, precisely, without exaggeration, without prejudice — the fact just as it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies across reporting of sports, sermons, lectures, etc. Reporting must be accurate and free from exaggeration; accuracy is 'one of the first and most precious ends of a good education.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Know how and where to look for what you don't know
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to know how and where most promptly to look for what you don't know and what you want to know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This information-seeking skill is ranked just after simple accuracy; cultivate habits of inquiry and sources-finding so you can promptly locate missing facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical faculty / sound judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Possess the critical faculty — the judgment which, when a proposition is stated or a fact is reported, looks at it calmly and says 'That is true' or 'That is false'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This cultivated instinct detects truth and error without long examination. The author cites Greeley as powerful in expression but sometimes deficient in this faculty — a cautionary example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough knowledge of the English language grounded in classical/Teutonic roots
rubrics_metrics.description: The man who does not know the old languages (Greek, Latin, and ideally Teutonic) does not really know the English language and does not command its resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical and Teutonic knowledge unlocks subtleties and expression in English; this is presented as foundational for a journalist's language competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate style (use of imagination, humor, and word-resources)
rubrics_metrics.description: After knowledge of English comes the cultivation of the ability to use it: the development of that art called style — a combination of imagination and humor with entire command of the word-resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style distinguishes writers but may be partially innate; practice can help but great perfection may be unacquirable by mere effort. Study exemplary writers (Channing, Hawthorne) to learn qualities like clarity and suggestiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity with politics, especially American politics
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of politics, and especially of American politics, is indispensable to anyone who means to fill an important place in journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes theory, doctrine, practical politics, history, key individuals, their ideas and deeds. Test of ambition: interest in political sections of papers versus romance reading. Practical political knowledge enables importance in public affairs reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the Constitution(s) and their principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Serious, calm, persistent study should be given to the Constitution of the United States (and to State constitutions) — not memorization but understanding the principles at the bottom of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know where the republic began and the impulse of the Constitution; understanding differences among state constitutions (e.g., elective vs appointed judiciary) improves judgment when conducting a newspaper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know European history (especially English history)
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern newspaper must look beyond its own country; study the history of England and of every European country, because the course of preparatory study is large and requires earnest attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding origins (e.g., English roots of American principles) and causes/effects in history (e.g., French history) helps interpret contemporary events; careful study is required, though one cannot learn everything at once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read indispensable books (Bible as professional manual)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are some books absolutely indispensable to the education of a journalist; chief among them is the Bible, considered as a manual of utility and professional preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Bible exemplifies 'sublime simplicity' and effective expression useful in controversy and principled argument; the text recommends opening and studying it for style and moral guidance, beyond strictly religious use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know Shakespeare and Milton (key English authors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Everybody going into the newspaper profession ought to know Shakespeare; John Milton's 'Speech for the Liberty of Unlicensed Printing' is also indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shakespeare is presented as the chief master of English speech; Milton provides foundational philosophy on the freedom of the press. These works are recommended as essential literary and philosophical preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop your own simple, clear style; avoid imitation and affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not take any model; every man has his own natural style. The thing to do is to develop it into simplicity and clearness and avoid affectation or imitation of others' mannerisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of bad imitation: trying to write like Matthew Arnold or Carlyle's influence leading to tedious imitation. Aim for your own clarity and follow honored literary traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting skills: learn facts, state them exactly, and enliven appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporter must learn accurately the facts and state them exactly as they are; reports must be accurate, free from affectation, well set forth, and, if possible, enlivened with imagination, feeling, or humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters are the 'eye of the paper' and must identify the vital fact(s) in a scene (e.g., which house's loss is greatest in a fire). Even if a reporter lacks grammar/spelling, precise factual capture and picturesque seeing can make work valuable after editorial polishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of selection: identify the vital fact in any story
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting an event the reporter must judge which is the most important thing about it (e.g., in a fire: which house, who suffered greatest loss, did anyone perish, how it happened).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is about prioritizing details that make the story newsworthy — the reporter must 'see' the picturesque, interesting, and important aspect and produce it clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exchange/newspaper reader: judgment and endurance in selecting extracts
rubrics_metrics.description: The man who reads other newspapers and makes extracts must know what should be taken from them and put into his paper; this requires judgment, knowledge, experience, and a sense of humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He may read thousands of papers daily and must pick interesting stories and nuances; it's a tiring but well-paid and important role. Anti-pattern: superficial skimming without discerning value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript editor skills: edit, correct, clarify, and select correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor who receives manuscripts must examine, prepare for the press, edit, correct slips of rhetoric, put right words or turns of phrase, clarify tangled facts, correct punctuation, and mark paragraph breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also responsible for correspondence selection (deciding whether a remote letter is publishable). This requires judgment, literary cultivation, and the ability to disentangle mixed presentation of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor-in-chief qualities: ability, character, and moral staying power
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor-in-chief attains position by natural selection because he can do the work; at the bottom of it all the lasting element is character as well as talent — moral staying power and honesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deceptive tricks may succeed briefly but won't last; people must believe the editor 'does not mean to say anything that is not so.' Leadership is both intellectual and moral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include scientific specialists on staff
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientific man who knows electricity, chemistry, and can understand inventions (e.g., Edison's) must be on a newspaper to cover scientific news of supreme consequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific literacy is a specialized department; without it the paper cannot competently report on technical inventions and discoveries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage news agencies (United Press) to cover global news
rubrics_metrics.description: The immense cost and necessity of gathering global news have led to agencies (e.g., the United Press) which supply the news of the whole world so individual editors can focus on local news and intellectual work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using such agencies reduces drudgery and expense of worldwide news collection, emancipating editors and writers to perform higher intellectual tasks; understand the economics and organization of news distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of practical experience and diverse newsroom roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Different newsroom functions (reporters, exchange readers, manuscript editors, scientific specialists) require distinct talents and training; practical practice in the profession is the best time to learn it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collegiate study should prepare one generally, but actual practice (reporting, editing, reading exchanges) refines skills. Example: many reporters earn well and learn on the job; combine formal education with hands-on newsroom experience.
